articles.title: In Moldova, teens are learning about democracy and elections through an app
articles.summary: VotEDU started off as a civic-education project to help young people understand democracy before they vote for the first time.
articles.content:
This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Moldova is a relatively small post-Soviet state with a population of three million people. A landlocked country, it has a long border with war-torn Ukraine and Romania; with the latter, it shares the same official language. The territory that is now Moldova was once part of the Russian Empire, and later the Soviet Union, and Russia has been meddling in its affairs.

Moldova has a large Russian-speaking population and a problematic unrecognized territory: Transnistria, which is basically controlled by Russia. It also has European aspirations and was officially named a candidate to join the European Union in 2022, after Russia invaded neighbouring Ukraine.

The country’s most recent parliamentary elections were held in September 2025, and despite the record influx of Russian disinformation and other meddling, elections were recognized as fair and democratic by the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OCSE) observers. The pro-European Party of Action and Solidarity (PAS) won the elections with a small majority.

The initiative supported by Digital Spark is an app called VotEDU, which answers basic questions about the democratic institution of elections for high school students in Moldova. It does so through short, interactive lessons using quizzes, flashcards, and other easily accessible formats in three languages: Romanian, Russian, and English, and is the subject of this Spotlight story.

Global Voices interviewed the app’s developer, Vlad Garbuz, about the impact of Digital Spark and his initiative.

Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project.

Vlad Garbuz (VG): I started VotEDU, an independent civic-education project in Moldova, to help young people understand democracy before they vote for the first time. The idea began at the VOTech hackathon in Moldova. I joined Digital Spark because I wanted to turn it into a tool that students could use in everyday life and teachers could bring into class. The project helped me build the app and begin testing it with the young people it is meant for.

GV: What issue or challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

VG: Young people meet politics every day through their feeds, long before they enter a polling station. In Moldova, many young people encounter misleading claims online. Yet many have very few easy ways of asking questions about elections and getting the answers they can understand. That made me wonder how civic education could reach young people in the spaces where they already spend their time. VotEDU was the answer. It puts short lessons, simple explanations, and activities on their phones, so they can learn at their own pace.

GV: What are the key changes or activities that you implemented during your participation in the project?

VG: During Digital Spark, VotEDU developed into a civic-education app with nine units, 28 short lessons, quizzes, interactive activities, and a glossary of 136 civic terms. The content is available in Romanian, Russian, and English. All of the lessons have been reviewed for accuracy and political neutrality. Student privacy guided the app’s design. A short guide was also prepared for teachers. VotEDU was represented at Moldova Digital Summit 2026, where several educators expressed interest in trying it in schools. The app is now being piloted with high school students in Moldova through its web version. It is also available on the App Store, with the Google Play version coming soon.

GV: How did your participation in the project impact your beneficiaries and the community you serve? Please provide examples.

VG: Teacher feedback has highlighted the need for digital tools alongside Moldova’s electoral education textbook. VotEDU brings these topics into a format students can explore on their phones. High school students in the pilot program are using the app and sharing feedback. The feedback tells us how easy the information was to access, as well as appreciation of the app’s design, quizzes, and illustrations. Together with teachers’ suggestions, this feedback is helping improve the content in the app and making it a better user experience.

GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed?

VG: I have learned that the design of a civic tool is part of its message. If an app is hard to understand, available in only one language, or careless with privacy, it may leave out the very people it hopes to reach. Building VotEDU has made me more careful about how I explain civic topics. Each lesson needs to be accurate and fair, while still being simple enough to use on a phone. I now think more about whether young people feel comfortable asking questions and forming their own views, not just whether the information is online.

GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

VG: The lesson I will carry forward is to start earlier. Young people should have a chance to understand democracy before an election campaign is asking for their attention. I have also learned that a good idea needs to be tested with the people it is meant to help. Building VotEDU was only one part of the work. Now students are using it and telling us what they think. Their experience will help us see what works, what is still unclear to students, and what needs to change.

GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built?

The app's multilingual, interactive design and pilot testing in schools demonstrate a meaningful, scalable impact on youth empowerment and democratic participation, benefiting the broader society.

articles.title: Leasehold system set to be scrapped in England and Wales
articles.summary: The proposed Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill will also include capping ground rent at £250.
articles.content:
The government is to introduce new laws to scrap the ownership rules for flats in England and Wales and cap ground rents at £250 a year.

Under the plans, which will not become law until at least next year, most new leasehold flats will eventually be banned and replaced with commonhold, where residents collectively own and manage their buildings.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook said the current leasehold system was "blighting lives" and was an "anachronism in the 21st century".

But the Residential Freehold Association says the plan is an "unprecedented abuse" of their rights, which will wipe billions from the value of pension funds, which have invested heavily in property.

The Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, to be published on Thursday, is likely to contain further details on when the measures would come into force.

In order to become law, the bill would first need to be approved by both Houses of Parliament, a process that will take several months.
articles.reasoning: The proposed legislation to scrap the leasehold system and cap ground rents represents a significant policy change aimed at improving housing rights and affordability for a broad population in England and Wales. It addresses a systemic issue affecting many residents, replacing a problematic ownership model with a more equitable commonhold system. The article provides sufficient context about the policy, its intended impact, and the legislative process, highlighting a meaningful improvement in quality of life for many people.
articles.personality_title: England and Wales to end leasehold system and limit ground rents
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In England and Wales, many people who own flats do so under a leasehold system. This means they have a lease from the freeholder, often paying yearly ground rent and facing restrictions on their property.

**What happened** – The government announced plans to stop the leasehold system for most new flats and introduce a new system called commonhold. Under commonhold, flat owners collectively own and manage their building without paying ground rent. The proposed Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill will also limit ground rent to £250 a year. These changes are expected to become law sometime next year after approval by Parliament.

**Impact** – This is a big change because many people have found the leasehold system unfair or expensive. By banning most new leaseholds and capping ground rents, the government aims to make home ownership clearer and cheaper. This could improve life for many residents who currently face high or rising charges. However, some investors worry about losing value in property funds.

**What's next step** – The bill will be published soon with more details and then debated in Parliament. It will take months before it becomes law. After that, the new rules will slowly replace leasehold with commonhold for new properties.

**One-sentence takeaway** – England and Wales plan to replace the leasehold system with commonhold and limit ground rents to make flat ownership fairer and less costly.
articles.personality_title_fr: L'Angleterre et le Pays de Galles vont supprimer le système de leasehold et limiter les loyers fonciers
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En Angleterre et au Pays de Galles, beaucoup de personnes possèdent des appartements sous un système appelé leasehold. Cela signifie qu'ils ont un bail du propriétaire foncier, paient souvent un loyer foncier annuel et font face à des restrictions sur leur bien.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Le gouvernement a annoncé son intention de supprimer le système de leasehold pour la plupart des nouveaux appartements et d'introduire un nouveau système appelé commonhold. Avec le commonhold, les propriétaires d'appartements possèdent et gèrent ensemble leur immeuble sans payer de loyer foncier. Le projet de loi sur la réforme du commonhold et du leasehold limitera aussi le loyer foncier à 250 £ par an. Ces changements devraient devenir loi l'année prochaine après approbation du Parlement.

**Impact** – C'est un grand changement car beaucoup trouvent le système de leasehold injuste ou coûteux. En interdisant la plupart des nouveaux leaseholds et en limitant les loyers fonciers, le gouvernement veut rendre la propriété plus claire et moins chère. Cela pourrait améliorer la vie de nombreux habitants qui paient aujourd'hui des charges élevées. Cependant, certains investisseurs craignent une perte de valeur dans leurs fonds immobiliers.

**Prochaine étape** – Le projet de loi sera bientôt publié avec plus de détails, puis débattu au Parlement. Il faudra plusieurs mois avant qu'il devienne loi. Ensuite, les nouvelles règles remplaceront progressivement le leasehold par le commonhold pour les nouvelles propriétés.

**Résumé en une phrase** – L'Angleterre et le Pays de Galles prévoient de remplacer le système de leasehold par le commonhold et de limiter les loyers fonciers pour rendre la propriété d'appartement plus juste et moins coûteuse.

**Contexto** – En Inglaterra y Gales, muchas personas poseen pisos bajo un sistema llamado leasehold. Esto significa que tienen un contrato de arrendamiento del propietario del terreno, pagan una renta anual y enfrentan restricciones sobre su propiedad.

En commonhold, los propietarios del piso poseen y gestionan juntos el edificio sin pagar renta del suelo. El proyecto de ley de Reforma de Commonhold y Leasehold también limitará la renta del suelo a 250 libras por año. Se espera que estas medidas se conviertan en ley el próximo año tras la aprobación del Parlamento.

**Impacto** – Este es un cambio importante porque muchas personas consideran que el sistema leasehold es injusto o caro. Al prohibir la mayoría de los nuevos leaseholds y limitar las rentas del suelo, el gobierno busca que ser propietario sea más claro y barato. articles.title: Family stories keep alive Georgia’s democratic past and the memory of Soviet repression
articles.summary: “Family stories can open up broader conversations about democracy, human rights, repression, and civic responsibility”
articles.content:
This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Guria is a region in Georgia, situated in the southwestern part of the country. It has a coastline on the Black Sea to the west, which is about 22 kilometers (13 miles) long, and the region is bordered by the Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti region to the north, Imereti to the east, and the Autonomous Republic of Adjara to the south. It has a rich history and a historical tradition of democracy.

Today, in the region, independent media access is limited and digital literacy remains low. However, Guria has a civic tradition that most of its own residents do not know about in detail.

In 1904, locals organized protests against imperial (Russian, at the time) institutions, formed institutions of self-governance, and proclaimed the Gurian Republic, an early experiment in participatory democracy.

The republic was violently suppressed first by the Russian tsarist empire, and later all the memories of it were fragmented further by decades of deliberate erasure under Soviet occupation of Georgia (1921–1991) and by repressions.

This is exactly what the Digital Spark Spotlight project in Georgia focused on: history and memory in the Guria region.

Global Voices interviewed Lika Mergaladze, head of the organization Komli Initiative for Civic Engagement, about their project: what they have done and what they learned through it.

Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project?

Lika Mergaladze (LM): Our organization, Komli Initiative for Civic Engagement, works to preserve local history, strengthen civic engagement, and promote sustainable development in the Guria region of Georgia. We use exhibitions, workshops, digital storytelling, and collaborative activities to connect communities with their history and encourage active participation in civic life. We chose to get involved in the Digital Spark project because we saw an opportunity to combine local history with modern digital technologies. We wanted to help community members document and share their family stories, develop digital skills, and better understand the connection between the past and present. We believe that preserving historical memory and encouraging critical thinking are essential for building an informed and active community.

GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

LM: One of the main challenges in Guria is that many important historical stories have been forgotten or remain untold. These stories were purposely erased during the Soviet Union. Many families who were the victims of a series of repressions in the 1920s and 30s learned to remain silent about their past in the 50s after World War II. As a result, younger generations often know very little about their ancestors and the region’s democratic traditions, including the Gurian Republic of 1904. Another challenge is limited access to independent media and low levels of digital literacy in local communities. The dominance of social media and television as information sources makes media literacy and critical thinking particularly important. We undertook this project to address these challenges by helping local people preserve their history, recognize misinformation and propaganda, and use digital tools to share their stories with a wider audience.

GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

LM: Through the project ‘From Understanding the Past to the Digital Future,’ implemented from April to October 2026, we organized several activities across the three municipalities of Guria: Ozurgeti, Chokhatauri, and Lanchkhuti. Our main activities included a public discussion. On June 24, we organized ‘What Drove Gurians Crazy? Propaganda Now and Then,’ exploring Guria’s democratic history, Soviet occupation, propaganda, and contemporary challenges. We also did digital storytelling workshops, an AI and Digital Creation workshop and a theatrical performance: on August 12, we presented “My Days and My Father’s Diaries,” dedicated to Meri Chanukvadze and her father, Amberki Chanukvadze, whose life reflected the impact of Soviet repression. These activities helped strengthen participants’ digital skills, encourage historical research, and create opportunities for community members to share their stories online.

GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

LM: The project generated strong interest across all three municipalities, reaching nearly 50 community members, with particularly strong participation from women and young people. Locals participated in the digital storytelling workshop, including 12 women. These activities gave participants practical opportunities to develop their digital skills and explore new ways of communicating important ideas. Another meaningful example was the theatrical performance dedicated to Meri and her father. More than 35 people attended and participated in a discussion afterwards. The performance encouraged people to reflect on the experiences of families affected by Soviet repression and the importance of preserving historical memory. The project also laid the foundation for a cross-municipal network of young people, activists, and aspiring digital storytellers. This network can help community members continue documenting local history, sharing civic information, and engaging in public discussions beyond the project itself.

GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

LM: Our participation in the project strengthened our understanding of how digital technologies can support civic engagement and democratic participation. We gained greater awareness of the importance of digital storytelling, media literacy, and critical thinking in helping communities understand their history and respond to contemporary challenges. We also explored how AI-assisted content creation can provide new opportunities for preserving local stories and making them accessible to wider audiences. The project reinforced our belief that digital tools are not simply communication technologies; they can also help people participate in public life, challenge misinformation, and contribute to community development. Most importantly, we recognized that connecting historical memory with modern digital tools can help create a more informed, active, and engaged society.

GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

LM: One of the most valuable lessons was that many people are interested in learning about their history when they are given a welcoming space to ask questions and share experiences. Family stories can open up broader conversations about democracy, human rights, repression, and civic responsibility. We also learned that practical workshops and collaborative activities are effective ways to introduce digital tools to community members. The strong participation of women and young people demonstrated the potential for inclusive, community-based learning. Another important lesson was the value of combining traditional storytelling with digital technologies. Personal stories, family diaries, public discussions, and theatrical performances can make historical events more relatable and meaningful.

GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?
articles.reasoning: The article describes a meaningful community-driven project in Georgia that preserves historical memory of democratic traditions and Soviet repression through digital storytelling and civic engagement. It has a broad societal impact by fostering media literacy, critical thinking, and active citizenship in a region with limited independent media access. The project empowers women and youth, strengthens democratic values, and combats misinformation, making it a significant positive contribution to human rights and democracy.

**What happened** – The Komli Initiative for Civic Engagement in Guria started a project from April to October 2026 to revive these lost stories. **What's next step** – The Komli Initiative plans to continue using digital tools to support civic engagement and historical memory in Guria. The network of young activists will help document local history and encourage public discussions beyond the project timeframe.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A community project in Georgia’s Guria region uses digital storytelling to revive forgotten democratic history and empower citizens with media skills.

articles.personality_title_es: La región de Guria en Georgia revive su historia perdida a través de relatos digitales
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Guria es una región en el suroeste de Georgia con una historia de movimientos democráticos tempranos. Compartieron historias familiares sobre la represión soviética y las tradiciones democráticas de la región.

**Impacto** – El proyecto alcanzó a casi 50 personas en tres municipios, permitiéndoles reconectarse con un pasado olvidado. Les dio herramientas para identificar la desinformación y compartir sus historias en línea. Una obra de teatro sobre una familia afectada por la represión soviética reunió a la comunidad para reflexionar. El proyecto también creó una red de jóvenes narradores digitales para mantener vivas estas conversaciones.

**Próximo paso** – La Iniciativa Komli planea continuar usando herramientas digitales para apoyar la participación cívica y la memoria histórica en Guria. La red de jóvenes activistas ayudará a documentar la historia local y a fomentar discusiones públicas más allá del proyecto.

**Una frase clave** – Un proyecto comunitario en la región de Guria, Georgia, utiliza relatos digitales para revivir una historia democrática olvidada y empoderar a los ciudadanos con habilidades mediáticas.

articles.title: An AI chatbot can explain your rights. But can it get you justice?
articles.summary: AI could make the law easier to navigate. But the real test is whether it helps people resolve the problems they face, not simply access information about their rights.
articles.content:
By Zainab Malik

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Imagine a woman facing eviction who turns to an AI chatbot for help. It explains her rights and drafts a letter to her landlord. But she cannot afford a lawyer, does not know where to submit the letter and has no institution that can enforce her rights fairly. The chatbot has made the law easier to understand, but has it brought her any closer to justice?

A September 2026 study by UK organization JUSTICE and the Administrative Fairness Lab found that one in six UK respondents who had experienced a legal dispute had used an AI chatbot. Researchers examined 77 conversations involving questions about rights, legal correspondence, complaints and court proceedings. Yet they could not establish whether these interactions helped resolve the disputes. We know more about how people use AI for legal help than whether it changes their circumstances.

That distinction matters. An estimated 1.5 billion people worldwide cannot obtain justice for their problems. HiiL’s Justice Needs Surveys, covering more than 150,000 people across 20 countries, show that only around four in 10 achieve a fair resolution. AI could help address this gap, but it is important to understand where its contribution begins and ends.

The promise of AI for justice seekers

People facing legal problems may not know whether what happened to them is unlawful, where to seek help or how to navigate an unfamiliar process. Legal advice is expensive, services can be difficult to reach, and institutions intimidating.

Purpose-built AI tools can explain rights clearly, organize information, prepare documents and identify relevant services. Voice-based tools may also reach people with limited literacy or without smartphones or reliable internet.

Early pilots are yielding promising results. In Australia, Hear Me Out, developed by the National Justice Project and the University of New South Wales, helps people identify the appropriate complaints body, understand the process and prepare supporting documents. Its pilot assisted more than 400 complaints, helping people turn experiences of injustice into complaints that can be pursued. In Nigeria, Citizens’ Gavel’s Podus AI helps people understand their legal rights, draft petitions and complaints, and identify the government agencies responsible for addressing them. Since its launch in March 2024, the platform has onboarded more than 33,000 users.

These are meaningful developments. But the number of tools and people assisted tells us only part of the story. What happens after someone submits a complaint?

When an answer is not a resolution

Understanding rights does not mean being able to exercise them. A tenant may know an eviction is unlawful but have nowhere to turn; a small business owner may prepare a claim but lack the means to pursue it. A person experiencing domestic abuse may face practical, financial or safety barriers to seeking protection.

Another challenge is getting the other party to participate. In dispute resolution, this is known as the “submission problem,” a concept developed by economists William Landes and Richard Posner. A process works only if both parties are willing to negotiate, accept mediation, or submit to a third-party decision. AI may help prepare a claim, but it cannot persuade a landlord to negotiate, compel an employer to pay wages, or make a business respond. Even when parties reach an agreement, there is no guarantee it will be respected. Without mechanisms to support compliance and enforce outcomes, an agreement on paper may have little practical effect.

There is also a growing challenge for the institutions receiving complaints. AI may make it much easier for people to submit them, potentially increasing demand on already overstretched public services. Recent UK reporting describes public bodies, councils and courts receiving a growing volume of AI-assisted submissions, some lengthy, repetitive and difficult to assess. Dubbed “AI clog,” the issue is not that more people are complaining — lowering barriers to redress is positive. The problem is that institutions may lack the capacity and resources to respond.

If AI increases the number of people approaching public authorities, those authorities must be equipped to meet the demand. This requires more than using AI to summarize documents or automate responses. It means better-designed complaints processes, adequately resourced institutions, trained staff and clear pathways for handling cases. Otherwise, technology risks making it easier to submit a complaint without making public services any more responsive.

Who owns the service?

Sustainability is another concern. A HiiL policy brief highlights the dependence of AI tools on external providers, proprietary platforms and uncertain funding. If a provider withdraws a service, what happens to the people relying on it?

HiiL’s exploration of voice-based AI support for local justice actors in Niger illustrates this risk. The aim was to make legal information available in local languages and support community intermediaries. But technology embedded in proprietary infrastructure can be difficult to maintain or transfer when a provider withdraws.

Ownership and governance therefore cannot be afterthoughts. Local justice providers and institutions need control over their tools, legal knowledge and data, as well as the resources to maintain and adapt services. Otherwise, technology intended to improve justice delivery may create new dependencies and disappear when people need it.

Making AI work for people seeking justice

AI for justice should be measured by more than chatbots launched, queries answered or documents generated. We need evidence that tools help people prevent problems, reach appropriate services, secure the participation of other parties and achieve fair outcomes.

This requires investment in tools designed around people’s problems and the providers best placed to address them. AI should connect users to human assistance, complement formal and informal justice mechanisms, and be supported by safeguards, accountability and sustainable financing. Crucially, public institutions must also be equipped to handle the increased demand that easier complaints procedures may generate. Evaluation should ask whether AI improves outcomes, for whom, under what conditions and at what cost. AI can make legal help more accessible and help people take action. But its promise will depend on whether the wider justice system can respond.

The ambition should not be to give everyone a free AI lawyer while leaving them waiting for an answer from the institutions responsible for upholding their rights. It should be to use technology to help those institutions work better, address people’s needs and deliver on their responsibilities fairly and effectively.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the promising use of AI tools to improve access to legal rights and justice for millions globally who currently face barriers. It discusses real-world pilot projects that have helped thousands understand and act on their rights, addressing a significant societal challenge of justice accessibility. The story focuses on a meaningful topic with detailed context, emphasizing the potential and limitations of AI in justice systems and the need for institutional support to achieve fair outcomes.
articles.personality_title: AI chatbots help people understand their rights, but justice needs more than technology
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many people around the world face legal problems but find it hard to get help. Legal advice can be expensive and confusing, and official services are often difficult to reach or slow. New AI tools are being developed to explain rights and guide people through legal processes.

**What happened** – Recent studies and pilot projects in countries like the UK, Australia, and Nigeria show that AI chatbots can explain legal rights, help draft letters or complaints, and point users to the right places for help. For example, an Australian tool helped over 400 people make complaints, and a Nigerian platform has supported more than 33,000 users since 2024.

**Impact** – These AI tools make legal information easier to understand and more accessible, especially for people who might not have smartphones or strong reading skills. However, knowing your rights is not the same as getting justice. Many people still cannot afford lawyers or face challenges in getting others to respond fairly. Also, public services may struggle to handle the growing number of AI-assisted complaints.

**What's next step** – To truly improve justice, AI tools must connect users to real support and work alongside better-funded and prepared institutions. Future efforts should focus on making sure public services can manage more cases, that tools are reliable and controlled locally, and that AI helps people achieve fair results, not just understand their rights.

**One-sentence takeaway** – AI chatbots can explain legal rights and guide people, but lasting justice depends on stronger support from real-world institutions and fair processes.

articles.personality_title_es: Los chatbots de IA explican tus derechos, pero la justicia necesita más que tecnología
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchas personas en el mundo enfrentan problemas legales pero tienen dificultades para recibir ayuda. Los consejos legales suelen ser caros y confusos, y los servicios oficiales son difíciles de acceder o lentos. Se están desarrollando nuevas herramientas de IA para explicar los derechos y guiar a las personas en los procesos legales.

**Qué pasó** – Estudios recientes y proyectos piloto en Reino Unido, Australia y Nigeria muestran que los chatbots de IA pueden explicar los derechos, ayudar a redactar cartas o quejas y señalar los lugares adecuados para pedir ayuda. Por ejemplo, una herramienta australiana ayudó a más de 400 personas a presentar quejas, y una plataforma nigeriana ha apoyado a más de 33,000 usuarios desde 2024.

**Impacto** – Estas herramientas de IA facilitan la comprensión y el acceso a la información legal, especialmente para quienes no tienen teléfono inteligente o tienen dificultades para leer. Sin embargo, conocer los derechos no es lo mismo que obtener justicia. Muchas personas no pueden pagar abogados o enfrentan problemas para lograr que otros respondan de forma justa. Además, los servicios públicos pueden estar saturados por el aumento de quejas asistidas por IA.

**Próximo paso** – Para mejorar realmente la justicia, las herramientas de IA deben conectar a los usuarios con apoyo real y trabajar junto a instituciones mejor financiadas y preparadas. Se debe asegurar que los servicios públicos puedan manejar más casos, que las herramientas sean confiables y controladas localmente, y que la IA ayude a lograr resultados justos, no solo a entender los derechos.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Los chatbots de IA pueden explicar los derechos legales y guiar a las personas, pero la justicia duradera depende de un mayor apoyo de las instituciones reales y procesos justos.
